# Humor, Idioms, and Slang

## Core Vocabulary

### Common Idioms
| Spanish | English | Example Sentence | Notes |
|---------|---------|-----------------|-------|
| no tener pelos en la lengua | to not mince words | Ella no tiene pelos en la lengua — dice todo lo que piensa. | Literally "to have no hairs on the tongue." Describes blunt honesty. |
| meter la pata | to put one's foot in it | Metí la pata al mencionar a su ex. | Literally "to stick the leg/paw in." Universal across dialects. |
| estar como una cabra | to be crazy / nuts | | Literally "to be like a goat." Affectionate, not clinical. Spain-origin but widely understood. |
| tomar el pelo | to pull someone's leg | ¿Me estás tomando el pelo? | Literally "to take the hair." Means to joke at someone's expense or deceive playfully. |
| dar en el clavo | to hit the nail on the head | | Literally "to hit the nail." Exact English equivalent. |
| ponerse las pilas | to get one's act together | Tienes que ponerte las pilas con el español. | Literally "to put in one's batteries." Very common, slightly informal. |
| no tener ni idea | to have no idea | | More emphatic than **no saber** |
| costar un ojo de la cara | to cost an arm and a leg | | Literally "to cost an eye from the face." Different body part than English. |
| echar una mano | to lend a hand | | Close to English — **echar**, not **dar** |
| ir al grano | to get to the point | Vamos al grano — ¿qué necesitas? | Literally "to go to the grain." |
| llevarse bien / mal | to get along / not get along | Nos llevamos muy bien desde el primer día. | Reflexive. Essential for describing relationships. |

## Common Collocations
- **contar un chiste** — to tell a joke; not **decir un chiste** (though understood)
- **gastar una broma** — to play a prank; **gastar**, not **hacer** (though **hacer una broma** is also used)
- **tener sentido del humor** — to have a sense of humor; uses **tener**
- **morirse de risa** — to die laughing; reflexive, hyperbolic
- **partirse de risa** — to crack up (Spain); less common in Latin America
- **caer bien / caer mal** — to like / dislike someone; NOT a fall — means "to land well/badly" socially
- **tomar a broma** — to take as a joke; **No lo tomes a broma** = Don't take it lightly

## False Cognates and Tricky Translations
- **gracioso/a** vs **gracious**: **Gracioso** means funny, not gracious. A gracious person is **amable** or **cortés**.
- **la broma** vs **broom**: Completely unrelated. A broom is **una escoba**.
- **el humor** vs **humor**: Close match, but **humor** in Spanish also means "mood" (**estar de buen/mal humor** = to be in a good/bad mood). The English "humor" (comedy) maps to **humor** and **sentido del humor**.
- **irónico** vs **ironic**: Same meaning, but Spanish speakers use **irónico** more precisely — for true situational irony, not just coincidence. English "ironic" is used more loosely.
- **sarcástico** vs **sarcastic**: Direct cognate, same meaning. But tone markers differ — Spanish sarcasm relies more on intonation and less on deadpan delivery.

## Dialect Variations
- **Slang is the most dialect-specific vocabulary.** Using Mexican slang in Argentina (or vice versa) marks you immediately as either foreign or from that region. Universal alternatives exist for all items.
- **Universal equivalents**: **genial** (cool — everywhere), **tío/a** (Spain) vs **güey** (Mexico) vs **boludo** (Argentina) vs **parcero** (Colombia) for "dude/buddy."
- **Idiom variation**: Most idioms listed are understood across all regions, but some are used more in specific areas. **Estar como una cabra** is more Spain. **Ponerse las pilas** is universal.
- **Diminutives as humor**: In Mexican Spanish, diminutives (**-ito/-ita**) are used humorously and affectionately in ways that would sound strange in other dialects. **Ahorita** (right now, but softer), **cerquita** (nearby), **tantito** (a tiny bit).

## Cultural and Pragmatic Notes
- **Register shifting is survival**: This cluster is inseparable from D-05 (register shifting). Using slang in the wrong context is worse than not knowing it. **Güey** with friends is bonding; with a stranger, it is offensive. **Boludo** between friends is warmth; directed at a stranger, it is an insult.
- **Humor as social currency**: Being able to joke — even badly — in someone's language signals respect and effort. Learners who try humor are received more warmly than those who speak perfectly but humorlessly.
- **Self-deprecating humor**: Very effective as a learner. "Perdón, mi español es un desastre" said with a smile builds rapport. But avoid overdoing it — constant self-deprecation becomes tiresome.
- **Idiom comprehension vs production**: Understand all idioms in this list; actively USE only the universal ones (**meter la pata**, **dar en el clavo**, **ponerse las pilas**). Using region-specific idioms as a non-native requires confidence and familiarity.
- **Dark humor tolerance**: Humor about death, religion, and politics is more accepted in most Spanish-speaking cultures than in mainstream American English. Expect it; do not react with shock.

## Pronunciation Alerts
- **güey** — one syllable: GUEY (like "way" with a hard G). The dieresis (**ü**) indicates the U is pronounced. Without it, **gue** would be "geh."
- **chido** — two syllables: CHI-do. The **ch** is one sound, not two.
- **órale** — stress on first syllable: Ó-ra-le. Rapid speech often reduces to "ORLE."
- **boludo** — three syllables: bo-LU-do. Not BO-lu-do.
- **ironía** — stress on the **í**: i-ro-NÍ-a. Four syllables. The written accent breaks the diphthong.
- **sarcasmo** — stress on second syllable: sar-CAS-mo. Not SAR-cas-mo.
